title: Imports and Dependencies
content: The formalization imports four key Mathlib modules: `Matrix.Charpoly.Minpoly` (the minimal polynomial of a matrix, including `minpoly.monic`, `minpoly.aeval`, `minpoly.dvd`, and `minpoly_dvd_charpoly`), `Matrix.Charpoly.Basic` (characteristic polynomial foundations), `Algebra.Polynomial.Div` (the division algorithm for polynomials, including `modByMonic_add_div` and `degree_modByMonic_lt`), and `RingTheory.Polynomial.Basic` (ring-theoretic properties of polynomial rings).
mathContext: Key Mathlib facts used: $\text{minpoly}(K, M)$ is monic, $\text{aeval}_M(\text{minpoly}) = 0$, $\text{minpoly} \mid \text{charpoly}$, and the division algorithm $f = q \cdot g + r$ with $\deg(r) < \deg(g)$ for monic $g$.

title: Minimal Polynomial Reduction Theorem
content: The core theorem: evaluating any polynomial $f$ at matrix $M$ equals evaluating the remainder $f \bmod \text{minpoly}(K, M)$. This is the matrix-algebra analogue of modular arithmetic: just as $a \equiv a \bmod n$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, we have $\text{aeval}_M(f) = \text{aeval}_M(f \bmod \text{minpoly})$. The proof applies the division algorithm $f = q \cdot \text{minpoly} + r$, evaluates at $M$, and uses $\text{aeval}_M(\text{minpoly}) = 0$ to eliminate the quotient term. The companion theorem shows $\text{aeval}_M(f - f \bmod \mu_M) = 0$.

title: Degree Bounds: Tighter than Charpoly
content: Two degree bound theorems establish the advantage of minpoly over charpoly reduction. First, $\deg(f \bmod \mu_M) < \deg(\mu_M)$ (from the division algorithm). Second, chaining with $\deg(\mu_M) \leq \deg(\chi_M) = n$, we get $\deg(f \bmod \mu_M) < n$. For **derogatory matrices** (where $\mu_M \neq \chi_M$), the bound $\deg(\mu_M) < n$ is strict, giving a genuinely tighter reduction. Example: a scalar matrix $cI$ has $\mu_M = X - c$ (degree 1) vs. $\chi_M = (X-c)^n$ (degree $n$).
mathContext: $\deg(f \bmod \mu_M) < \deg(\mu_M) \leq \deg(\chi_M) = n$. For derogatory $M$: $\deg(\mu_M) < n$, so minpoly reduction is strictly tighter.

title: Annihilator Ideal Characterization
content: The key structural result: $\text{aeval}_M(f) = 0$ if and only if $\mu_M \mid f$. This means the **annihilator** of $M$ in $K[X]$ is the principal ideal $(\mu_M)$. Since $K[X]$ is a PID (principal ideal domain), every ideal is principal, and $\mu_M$ is the unique monic generator of the annihilator. The proof establishes closure under addition and multiplication (making it an ideal) and uses Mathlib's `minpoly.dvd` for the key direction. The converse follows from $\text{aeval}_M(\mu_M) = 0$ and multiplicativity of evaluation.
mathContext: $\ker(\text{aeval}_M : K[X] \to M_n(K)) = (\mu_M) = \{f \in K[X] : \mu_M \mid f\}$. This is a principal ideal in the PID $K[X]$.

title: Congruence Modulo Minimal Polynomial
content: Two polynomials $f$ and $g$ evaluate to the same matrix iff $\mu_M \mid (f - g)$, i.e., $f \equiv g \pmod{\mu_M}$. This defines an equivalence relation on $K[X]$ whose classes correspond 1-to-1 with elements of the subalgebra $K[M] = \{p(M) : p \in K[X]\}$. The quotient $K[X]/(\mu_M)$ is isomorphic to $K[M]$ as a $K$-algebra, with $\dim_K K[M] = \deg(\mu_M)$. This is a finer equivalence than charpoly congruence since $\mu_M \mid \chi_M$.
mathContext: $\text{aeval}_M(f) = \text{aeval}_M(g) \iff \mu_M \mid (f - g) \iff f \equiv g \pmod{\mu_M}$. Quotient: $K[X]/(\mu_M) \cong K[M] \subseteq M_n(K)$.

title: Power Reduction via Minimal Polynomial
content: Every matrix power $M^k$ can be expressed as a polynomial in $M$ of degree $< \deg(\mu_M)$: $M^k = \text{aeval}_M(X^k \bmod \mu_M)$. This means $\{I, M, M^2, \ldots, M^{d-1}\}$ (where $d = \deg(\mu_M)$) spans the subalgebra $K[M]$. For computing $M^{100}$ when $d = 3$, we only need to find $X^{100} \bmod \mu_M$ (a degree $\leq 2$ polynomial), then evaluate the 3-term expression. This is the basis of efficient matrix exponentiation.
mathContext: $M^k = \text{aeval}_M(X^k \bmod \mu_M)$, so $M^k = \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} c_i M^i$ where $d = \deg(\mu_M)$. The set $\{I, M, \ldots, M^{d-1}\}$ is a $K$-basis of $K[M]$.

title: Comparison with Characteristic Polynomial Reduction
content: Three results establish the relationship between minpoly and charpoly reductions. (1) $\deg(\mu_M) \leq \deg(\chi_M) = n$. (2) $\deg(\mu_M) > 0$ (the minpoly is never constant). (3) **Refinement**: reducing first by $\chi_M$ then by $\mu_M$ gives the same result as reducing directly by $\mu_M$. Since $\mu_M \mid \chi_M$, the minpoly reduction is always at least as tight. For nonderogatory matrices ($\mu_M = \chi_M$), both reductions coincide.
mathContext: $\deg(\mu_M) \leq \deg(\chi_M) = n$ and $\text{aeval}_M(f \bmod \chi_M) = \text{aeval}_M(f \bmod \mu_M)$ for all $f$. Nonderogatory: $\mu_M = \chi_M \Leftrightarrow \deg(\mu_M) = n$.

title: Special Cases: Scalar, Identity, and Zero Matrices
content: Concrete examples showing the minpoly-charpoly gap. The identity matrix $I$ satisfies $X - 1$ (degree 1), while $\chi_I = (X-1)^n$. The zero matrix satisfies $X$ (degree 1), while $\chi_0 = X^n$. More generally, scalar matrices $cI$ satisfy $X - c$. These are maximally derogatory: $\deg(\mu_M) = 1$ while $\deg(\chi_M) = n$.
mathContext: $\mu_I = X - 1$, $\mu_0 = X$, $\mu_{cI} \mid X - c$. In each case $\deg(\mu_M) = 1 \ll n = \deg(\chi_M)$.

title: Nilpotent Matrices via Minimal Polynomial
content: A matrix $M$ with $\mu_M = X^d$ is nilpotent of index exactly $d$: $M^d = 0$ and $M^{d-1} \neq 0$. The proof substitutes $\mu_M = X^d$ into $\text{aeval}_M(\mu_M) = 0$ to get $M^d = 0$. Higher powers vanish by $M^k = M^d \cdot M^{k-d} = 0$. The nilpotency index equals $\deg(\mu_M)$, which is more precise than using $\chi_M = X^n$ (which only gives $M^n = 0$).
mathContext: $\mu_M = X^d \Rightarrow M^d = 0$, and $\forall k \geq d,\; M^k = 0$. The nilpotency index $= d = \deg(\mu_M) \leq n = \deg(\chi_M)$.

title: Polynomial Identities via Annihilator Theory
content: The annihilator ideal structure provides a systematic method for proving matrix identities: to show $\text{aeval}_M(f) = \text{aeval}_M(g)$, it suffices to show $\mu_M \mid (f - g)$. The theorem `aeval_eq_of_minpoly_dvd_diff` formalizes this. Additionally, `annihilating_degree_ge_minpoly` shows that any nonzero annihilating polynomial has degree $\geq \deg(\mu_M)$, confirming the minimality of $\mu_M$.
mathContext: If $f - g = \mu_M \cdot q$ then $\text{aeval}_M(f) = \text{aeval}_M(g)$. For nonzero $f$ with $\text{aeval}_M(f) = 0$: $\deg(f) \geq \deg(\mu_M)$.

title: Idempotent and Involutory Matrix Classification
content: **Idempotent matrices** ($M^2 = M$): $M$ satisfies $X^2 - X = X(X-1)$, so $\mu_M \mid X(X-1)$. Since $X(X-1)$ has distinct roots over any field, $\mu_M \in \{X, X-1, X(X-1)\}$ — corresponding to $M = 0$, $M = I$, or a nontrivial projection. **Involutory matrices** ($M^2 = I$): $M$ satisfies $X^2 - 1 = (X-1)(X+1)$, so $\mu_M \mid (X-1)(X+1)$. If $\text{char}(K) \neq 2$, the factors are distinct, giving $\mu_M \in \{X-1, X+1, (X-1)(X+1)\}$ — corresponding to $M = I$, $M = -I$, or a nontrivial involution.
mathContext: Idempotent: $M^2 = M \Rightarrow \mu_M \mid X(X-1)$, so $\mu_M \in \{X, X-1, X(X-1)\}$. Involutory: $M^2 = I \Rightarrow \mu_M \mid (X-1)(X+1)$.

title: Summary of Results
content: The summary section lists all 25+ theorems organized into categories: the core reduction theorem, degree bounds, annihilator ideal characterization, congruence results, power reduction, charpoly comparison, and special matrix classes (idempotent, involutory, nilpotent). The `#check` commands verify the key theorem signatures. All results are fully proved with 0 sorries, building on Mathlib's foundational results for minimal and characteristic polynomials.
